name: Gosain otoplasty

lead: The Gosain technique is an otoplasty (ear surgery) approach named after surgeon Arun Gosain. In reference descriptions it is used for the earlobe: a prominent lobule that flares outward is repositioned nearer the head by closing a medial skin incision while taking a bite of the underside of the concha. The goal is ears that sit in proportion with no visible sign of surgery.

Online it is sometimes described as a method that combines cartilage scoring with sutures; the sources consulted describe scoring and suturing as separate, widely used otoplasty methods and attribute the lobule repositioning to Gosain. Reference descriptions note that moving the lobule is the most difficult part of otoplasty.

paras: The technique is performed by a surgeon, typically alongside an antihelical fold correction, in an outpatient or inpatient setting under local or general anesthesia. Recovery generally involves a loose dressing for several days and a snug headband during sleep for three to six weeks, with swelling and bruising settling in about two weeks.

Reported otoplasty complications include overcorrection and unnatural contours, suture extrusion (the most common complication overall), hematoma that needs prompt drainage, and infection that can progress to chondritis and permanently deform the ear. Anyone considering surgery would discuss risks with a qualified surgeon.

angle.text: The procedure is intended to make a protruding lobule lie closer to the head, which changes the ear's silhouette from the front and the side. It is usually part of a wider otoplasty.

lead: The Gosain technique is a surgical method for correcting a prominent earlobe within the wider family of otoplasty procedures, also called ear pinning. It is named for plastic surgeon Arun Gosain. Wikipedia names the Gosain technique, or a variant of it, as the most effective method for moving a prominent lobule closer to the head, and describes it as closing a medial skin incision while taking a bite of the concha's underside [1].

People interested in changing how their ears look consider otoplasty to reduce ear prominence, because ears that flare from the head can draw attention to the side profile and frontal view. The lobule has no cartilage, so correcting it usually calls for a step separate from creating the antihelical fold with sutures or scoring [1].

Some online descriptions label the technique as combining scoring and sutures. Published reference descriptions treat scoring (the Stenström approach), suturing (Mustardé, Merck) and combined methods as distinct families, and place Gosain's name on lobule repositioning [1].

paras: Otoplasty methods fall into suture techniques, cartilage scoring, full-thickness incisions, conchal alteration and earlobe repositioning [1]. Gosain's method sits in the last group: the surgeon closes a medial skin incision and takes a bite of the underside of the concha so the lobule is drawn toward the head [1]. Wikipedia calls lobule repositioning the most difficult part of otoplasty [1].

Ear surgery is described in the Sushruta Samhita (around 500 AD), Dieffenbach reported a surgical approach for prominent ears in 1845, Ely performed ear pinback surgery in 1881, and Mustardé published his suture technique in 1963 [1]. Surgery for children is commonly done around age 5 to 6 when the ear is near adult size [1].

Operations last about 1.5 to 5 hours. Swelling and bruising generally subside within about two weeks, and a snug headband is worn during sleep for 3 to 6 weeks [1]. Overcorrection and unnatural contour are described as the most significant complication, suture extrusion as the most common, with hematoma, infection and chondritis possible [1].
No studies found that evaluate the Gosain technique by name in the sources consulted. Otoplasty as a category has an extensive surgical literature.

Otoplasty entries are discussed in hardmaxxing sections as ways to correct prominent ears. Technique names such as Mustardé, Stenström, Furnas and Gosain appear in surgeon-consultation discussions as vocabulary.

timeline.event: Dieffenbach reports a surgical approach for prominent ears [1].
